rationale: Xenopus experiments support teratogen-induced disruption of neural bioelectric patterns and substantial rescue by HCN2-mediated voltage correction. The compound claim is somewhat stronger because it joins morphological, molecular, and behavioral rescue across three distinct insults.

Loss of coordination with surrounding tissue is a plausible and useful description of malignant cells. Calling this a smaller self or cognitive light cone is chiefly a theoretical interpretation, not an established explanation of cancer across multicellular animals.

Reduced gap-junctional communication is common in early transformation, and tissue architecture can constrain neoplastic behavior. The proposed self-reinforcing computational loop remains mechanistically underdetermined, and geometric-barrier tumors do not by themselves establish it.

Oncogene-expressing Xenopus tissues have been reported to show characteristic membrane-voltage changes before overt tumor-like growth, allowing early fluorescent voltage imaging. This supports detection in the narrow experimental scope, though not necessarily unique cancer specificity.

Transient manipulation of ion transport and serotonergic signaling in Xenopus can drive melanocyte overproliferation, altered morphology, and invasion resembling melanoma without an introduced oncogene or carcinogen. Demonstrating a complete absence of incidental DNA damage is harder, but it is not required as the initiating manipulation.

Forced hyperpolarization and manipulation of ion-channel states have suppressed or normalized oncogene-induced tumor-like phenotypes in Xenopus while oncogene expression persisted. The result is strong within this model, although normalization may be phenotypic rather than eradication of every transformed property.

Bioelectric state can override oncogene-driven phenotypes in some experimental systems, showing that genotype is not uniquely determinative. That does not establish that physiological information processing generally dominates cancer outcomes or justify a distinct human clinical roadmap.

Group-dependent signaling among Xenopus embryos can plausibly produce coordinated transcriptional changes and improved resistance to developmental perturbation. The strong wording about a distinct hyperembryo and far better resistance appears to rest on a narrow experimental context and needs broad replication.

A nonspecific ionophore can provide a permissive bioelectric trigger while positional and wound-context information in host tissues determines whether a tail or limb structure is regenerated. This is consistent with context-dependent regenerative patterning in Xenopus, though monensin is a trigger rather than proof that all specificity resides only in the collective.

Age-related loss of tissue-level electrical coordination is plausible and bioelectric signaling contributes to maintenance and repair. Evidence does not establish degradation of bioelectric pattern memories as a general cause of aging, so the proposal remains speculative.
